profile.feeling: A choice between two – and, at the end of a sentence, a friendly “right?”.

senses.def: right?, isn’t it? (tag at the end of a sentence)

examples.tr: Do you want tea or coffee?
The food is good, isn’t it?

phrases.text: Sein oder Nichtsein, das ist hier die Frage.
phrases.tr: To be or not to be, that is the question here.
phrases.source: Shakespeare, Hamlet, translated by A. W. Schlegel (1798), public domain

synonyms.nuance: or rather, respectively – written and official language

etymology.text: From Middle High German oder, from Old High German odar, an alteration of odo by analogy with wedar (whence modern weder). The origin of odo is uncertain; compare Old English eþþa, oþþe and Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌸𐌰𐌿 (aiþþau).

funFacts: oder got its -r from weder (neither) – the two words influenced each other in Old High German.
pitfalls: oder does not change the word order: Willst du Tee oder Kaffee?
A question with oder is answered with the choice, not with ja or nein: Tee, bitte.
subtleties: …, oder? at the end asks for agreement, like English right? or Turkish değil mi? – very frequent in the south and in Switzerland.

senses.def: softener in polite requests (Können Sie mir vielleicht helfen?)
expresses amazement, often ironic (Du bist vielleicht lustig!)

synonyms.nuance: possibly, if need be – a false friend: not “eventually”

etymology.text: From Middle High German vil līchte (“very easily”), thus: “what could easily happen”. Compare Dutch wellicht.

funFacts: vielleicht is viel + leicht, “very easily”: what may easily happen. Greek ίσως, Russian может быть (“it may be”) and Turkish belki express the same idea differently.
pitfalls: When vielleicht starts the sentence, the verb comes second: Vielleicht trinke ich Tee (not *Vielleicht ich trinke Tee).
subtleties: In a request vielleicht makes it more polite: Hast du vielleicht ein bisschen Zeit?

profile.feeling: Surprise and interest (“Really?”) – or sincere emphasis.

senses.def: really? – a reaction of surprise or interest
real, actual (as an adjective: die wirkliche Welt)

examples.tr: Do you really not eat meat?

synonyms.nuance: really – the casual reaction, very common among young people: Echt?
actually, indeed; as a reaction: Tatsächlich? (Is that so?)

etymology.text: From wirk(en) + -lich. Cognate with Bavarian wirkli and Dutch werkelijk.

funFacts: wirklich comes from wirken (to work, to have an effect): what is real is what works – die Wirklichkeit is reality.
The reaction “Really?” is Wirklich? in German, Αλήθεια; in Greek, Правда? in Russian and Gerçekten mi? in Turkish.
pitfalls: As an adverb wirklich never changes; as an adjective (real) it takes endings: ein wirkliches Problem.
Wirklich? alone is a reaction; inside the sentence it emphasises: Das ist wirklich gut.
subtleties: nicht wirklich (not really) works much like English and softens a no.

profile.feeling: Self-evident, friendly agreement – sometimes a little impatient.

senses.def: naturally, in a natural way (also the adjective: natural)

examples.tr: Are you coming along? – Of course!

synonyms.nuance: sure, of course – the casual answer
it goes without saying – service language

etymology.text: From Middle High German natiurlich, from Old High German natūrlīh. Equivalent to Natur + -lich. Compare Dutch natuurlijk, English naturally.

funFacts: natürlich = “by nature”: Greek φυσικά (from φύση, nature) means both “naturally” and “of course” – exactly like German; English naturally does too.
pitfalls: At the start of a sentence it takes the first place and the verb comes second: Natürlich trinke ich Kaffee.
Said with a sharp tone it can sound like “obviously!” – softer: ja, gern.

senses.def: modal particle: really, in fact (Hast du auch alles?)

examples.tr: My brother is a teacher too.
Are you sure you have everything?

synonyms.nuance: likewise, also – and the polite reply “(the) same to you”
likewise – as a reply: Guten Appetit! – Danke, gleichfalls!

etymology.text: From Middle High German ouch, from Old High German ouh, from Proto-Germanic *auk. Cognate with Dutch ook (“also”), Swedish och (“and”), Danish og (“and”) and archaic English eke (“also”).

funFacts: auch is a cousin of archaic English eke (“also”) and of Swedish och and Danish og, which mean “and”.
pitfalls: auch stands before the word it adds: Ich trinke auch Tee (tea as well) – Auch ich trinke Tee (I too).
Me neither = Ich auch nicht (not *Ich auch kein).
subtleties: Unstressed, auch is a particle that checks: Hast du auch alles? (Are you sure you’ve got everything?)

senses.def: in wishes and urging: if only, just (Wenn ich nur Zeit hätte!)

examples.text: Wenn ich nur mehr Zeit hätte!
examples.tr: If only I had more time!

synonyms.nuance: only (so far) – with time and numbers when more is expected: Er ist erst drei.

etymology.text: From late Middle High German nuor, contracted from older niwer, newære, from Old High German niwāri, ni wāri (“were it not”). Cognate with Yiddish נאָר (nor), Dutch maar.

funFacts: nur grew out of ni wāri, “were it not” – the same origin as Dutch maar (“but”).
pitfalls: nur vs erst: Es ist erst acht Uhr (only eight – it will get later); Ich habe nur zehn Euro (only ten – that’s all).
nur stands before what it limits: Nur ich trinke Tee / Ich trinke nur Tee.
subtleties: Nur so! = Just because / for no special reason.

lexemes.role: yes – the answer that contradicts a negative question or statement (Isst du kein Fleisch? – Doch!)

profile.feeling: A confident contradiction: “Oh yes I do!”

senses.def: yes (contradicting a negative question or statement)
modal particle: after all, do (Komm doch mit!)

examples.tr: Don’t you eat meat? – Yes, I do!

examples.text: Du magst keinen Käse. – Doch, ich mag Käse!
examples.tr: You don’t like cheese. – Oh yes, I do like cheese!

synonyms.nuance: yes – after a negative question ja is unclear; doch makes the contradiction plain

etymology.text: From Middle High German doch, from Old High German doh, from Proto-West Germanic *þauh, from Proto-Germanic *þauh. Cognate to Old English þēah (English though).

funFacts: doch is a cousin of English though.
pitfalls: doch answers only a negative question or statement; to a positive question the answer is ja: Isst du Fleisch? – Ja.
Answering a negative question with nein agrees with it: Isst du kein Fleisch? – Nein (= No, I don’t).
subtleties: French si and Arabic بَلَى (balā) do the same job as doch; English needs a whole sentence (“Yes, I do!”).
